arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Goodhart argued temporary flooding can be a taking. He stated the Federal Circuit ruling that permanent consequences are irrelevant is incorrect. He asserted the lower-court rule cannot stand.
Mr. Kneedler argued temporary flooding is a trespass. He distinguished temporary flooding from permanent invasion cases. He cited precedent requiring permanent invasion for government responsibility.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case asks if temporary flooding by the government counts as a taking under the Fifth Amendment. the side that brought the case argues temporary flooding can be a taking. The government argues temporary flooding is never a taking. The lower court ruled temporary flooding is not a taking. the side that brought the case seeks to reverse that ruling. The government seeks to affirm that ruling.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if temporary flooding is a taking.

Justice Breyer asked how temporary flooding differs from permanent invasion cases like Causby and Kimball Laundry. Justice Breyer noted eleven cases support the temporary trespass view. Justice Ginsburg asked about the Sanguinetti precedent requiring permanent invasion for government responsibility.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether landowners can claim compensation for temporary government flooding. It defines the scope of the Fifth Amendment's takings clause. It clarifies the legal distinction between temporary trespass and permanent taking. It impacts government water management and property rights.
